Correlated level loss inverts the missing-level correction in quantum chaotic spectra

The standard correction for missing energy levels assumes they vanish at random. Real spectrometers lose the levels that sit too close to resolve — and that reverses the error rather than reducing it.

Henry Wang1, Albert Fei1, Leo Lee1, Finley Dou1, Jake Kim1

1Shanghai High School International Division, Shanghai, China |henry2023trp@gmail.com |PRISM working paper PRISM-WP-002

17 pages 6 figures 46 references 18,000 measured levels Preregistered

Download the full paper (PDF, 17 pp)

Abstract

Microscopic dynamics is reversible and macroscopic behaviour is not, and the modern account of the difference is quantum chaos: an isolated system forgets its initial state on a timescale set by the correlations between its energy levels. That timescale is therefore read out of measured spectra. We show that the standard procedure for doing so rests on a model of missing data that is wrong for every real spectrometer, and that the error runs in the opposite direction to the one assumed.

The established correction treats undetected levels as lost independently at random, which dilutes level repulsion and makes a chaotic spectrum look regular. Real instruments instead miss levels that lie too close to a neighbour to resolve, which removes small spacings and makes the same spectrum look more rigid. The two modes are not approximations of each other. At a surviving fraction of 0.60 the random-loss correction reports a complete spectrum: forty per cent of the levels are absent and the standard method finds none missing.

We prove that resolution-limited loss cannot receive the binomial noise term that destroys rigidity under random loss, because the filter is a deterministic function of the configuration, and we derive the resulting hard-core signature — a negative excursion of the two-level form factor near the Heisenberg time that random loss never produces. This identifies the loss mode from data alone, correctly in 160 of 160 simulated datasets, and yields a corrected inversion that recovers the surviving fraction without bias where the standard one saturates.

On 99,351 Riemann zeros, a spectrum complete by construction, the method returns 0.982 and selects unitary symmetry, as it must. Applied to 18,000 measured nuclear and atomic levels the estimator returns the same completeness, about 0.30, for opposite reasons: in nuclei the correlation hole deepens with excitation energy (P = 0.015), which is chaos setting in, while in atoms it shallows (P < 10−4), which is detection efficiency falling.

Status of this paper

Not peer reviewed

No referee independent of the author list has assessed this manuscript. Henry Wang is Editor-in-Chief of PRISM, and Albert Fei, Leo Lee, Finley Dou and Jake Kim hold editorial or refereeing roles on it, so none of them may referee it. It is posted as a working paper for that reason.

A statement of what each author contributed is also outstanding. The project repository records no allocation of work — the preregistration, the deviations file and the manuscript are written throughout in the first person plural — so no such statement can be made from the record.

Preregistration and deviations

The analysis targets, the controls and the analysis rules were fixed before any spectrum was loaded. The deviations file opens by recording that a preregistered literature check went against the authors: three of the four derivation targets turned out to be standard results already in the literature, and the contribution narrowed accordingly. That amendment is dated and was made before any manuscript text was written.

Data and code availability

All three spectra are public — the Odlyzko tables of Riemann zeros, the IAEA ENSDF service and the NIST Atomic Spectra Database. Fifteen scripts reproduce every number and figure from those downloads, and a sixteenth checks that every figure panel is cited in the text. The repository is not yet deposited in a public archive with a DOI, so the analysis cannot currently be recomputed by a reader.

Reference verification

The bibliography was resolved against Crossref on 25 September 2026 and every entry carries the DOI returned. References cited for standard results were verified to exist and to be correctly attributed; they were not read in full. One candidate reference was discarded because the record returned did not support the claim it was to be cited for.
